source.title: A rationale from frequency perspective for grokking in training neural network
source.authors: Zhang-Chen Zhou; Yaoyu Zhang; Zhi-Qin John Xu

record.tranche_reason: Tests delayed generalization and a proposed mechanism using frequency analyses on synthetic, parity, and MNIST experiments; it is not a direct reproduction of the original modular-arithmetic Transformer setup.
record.gate_note: Rows record the study's own loss, accuracy, error, and frequency-spectrum results. Values visible only in figures are recorded as figure only. Results cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study trains its own networks on parity, 1D synthetic regression and MNIST, reporting delayed test-loss or accuracy improvement. It varies training proportion, sampling and initialization scale, and offers a frequency-based mechanism instead of a circuit or regime account. It does not reproduce the original modular-arithmetic Transformer setup.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue empirically that grokking arises because insufficient or nonuniform sampling creates training-data frequency components not dominant in the test data. Networks fit these first: low frequencies under the F-Principle at default init, or all frequencies at a similar pace at large init. They add that Liu et al.'s explanation may not apply to their MNIST run without weight decay, and that they need no lazy-to-rich transition. The limitation is that the mechanism may not apply to language-based data, explicitly including the algorithmic datasets, and that no theory is given.
record.recipe_differences: Uses fully connected networks on one-dimensional synthetic data, parity, and MNIST, and studies frequency spectra; it does not reproduce the original modular-arithmetic Transformer experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome varies with sampling distribution and sample size in the synthetic experiment, parity training proportion, and MNIST initialization scale.

fits_no_version.finding: Grokking coincides with a mismatch between training-set and test-set frequency spectra caused by insufficient or nonuniform sampling. The network first fits spurious frequencies (low frequencies at default init; high-frequency aliasing at large init), then learns the true frequencies as test performance improves.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Frequency account: grokking arises when the training dynamics' frequency preference (F-Principle, or its breakdown at large init) favours spurious components introduced by undersampling, and generalization follows once the true dominant frequencies are learned.

record.problems: The frequency account is presented empirically without a comprehensive theoretical explanation. Many values are conveyed only in figures; numerical test accuracy and detailed timing are not stated in the text. The authors caution that the mechanism may not apply to language-based grokking.

untested.parts: The original modular-arithmetic and Transformer setting is not tested. Grokking is shown in MSE test loss, not a chance-to-perfect accuracy jump, and timings are figure-only.
No circuit identification, no memorizing-component removal, and no progress measure predicting the jump.
Text and molecule data, weight-norm manipulation, and an explicit lazy-to-rich transition are not tested.
Not tested; no weight decay, critical dataset size or ungrokking analysis.
Not tested; optimizers are not compared in a controlled way.

missing.what: Classification error curves for all parity training proportions (whether test error reaches zero at 0.2 and 0.8)
Output-function evolution on 1D synthetic data (near-zero, then sin x, then sin 6x)

record.verdict_notes: V1 verdict rests on parity, a small algorithmic task, but grokking is defined by MSE test loss rising then falling, and all timings are figure-only. The frequency-spectrum rows were relinked from V2 to none because they measure output spectra, not circuits or progress measures. The study's claim that grokking needs no regime transition (synthetic and parity cases) bears on V3's 'not the data' framing, hence limits_scope. Neither original source (2201.02177, 2301.05217) is this study.

versions.untested_parts: The text does not give exact chance-level test accuracy or training-accuracy saturation times for every split. The loss curves and classification error are reported, but only the 0.5 parity split is explicitly said to reach zero test error.

The study tracks frequency components, not an identified generalizing circuit or mechanistically identified memorizing circuit. It does not establish that a continuous progress measure predicts the accuracy jump.
The study tests non-algorithmic synthetic data and MNIST, and compares MNIST initialization scales. It does not test text or molecules, or a weight-norm sweep or lazy-to-rich transition.

relationships.condition: Non-algorithmic data: 1D sin 6x with nonuniform n=65 sampling (sin, ReLU, tanh), and MNIST with large init α=8 and no weight decay
relationships.reason: Delayed generalization appears on non-algorithmic data (R1, R15, R17, R11). It is absent at default init on MNIST (R12), consistent with init scale switching it.
relationships.display_finding: Delayed generalization appeared in synthetic regression and large-initialization MNIST training, while the default-initialization MNIST run showed no delay.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Non-algorithmic data: 1D sin 6x with nonuniform n=65 sampling (sin, ReLU, tanh), and MNIST with large init α=8 and no weight decay
source_check.reason: The text reports grokking on synthetic regression, asserts robustness across ReLU and tanh, and reports MNIST grokking with large initialization without explicit weight decay. This supports occurrence beyond algorithmic data; the MNIST comparison does not isolate initialization because optimizer and learning rate also change.

relationships.condition: 1D synthetic data at fixed default initialization, varying sample count and sampling distribution; MNIST comparison confounded by optimizer
relationships.reason: At default (small) init with no regime change, grokking is switched on or off by data sampling: present at nonuniform n=65, absent when uniform (R3) or n=1000 (R2, R16, R18). So data, not just regime, controls it. The MNIST α=8 vs α=1 runs also change optimizer (R11, R12).
relationships.display_finding: At fixed default initialization, grokking appeared with 65 nonuniform samples but disappeared with uniform sampling or 1,000 samples; MNIST comparisons also changed optimizer alongside α=8 versus α=1.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: 1D synthetic data at fixed default initialization, varying sample count and sampling distribution; MNIST comparison confounded by optimizer
source_check.reason: R1–R3 establish that changing sample count or sampling distribution changes grokking under the same default-initialization recipe. R11–R12 jointly change initialization, optimizer and learning rate. These qualify V3's exclusive regime explanation independently of the unverified absence states in R16 and R18.
